title: Resolving Wicked Problems
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece distinguishes ordinary hard problems from truly wicked ones: issues with two well-supported but competing solutions where picking a side risks lasting relational damage. Using the phonics-versus-whole-language reading debate as an illustration, the essay argues that wicked problems are less about intellectual complexity than about the interpersonal fallout of choosing one camp over another. It lays out a sequence for leaders to work through them without forcing a premature verdict: acknowledge the legitimacy of both sides publicly, involve stakeholders in that acknowledgment, gather deeper data on each option (including trial runs), and finally pursue what it calls Participatory Redesign, blending elements of both approaches rather than declaring a winner. The underlying message is that inflexibility, not the problem's inherent difficulty, is what turns a wicked problem into a lasting affliction.
points: Wicked problems are defined less by complexity than by the relational conflict that follows from choosing one side over another.
The first leadership move is public, neutral acknowledgment that both competing options have legitimate merit.
Trial programs and deliberate data-gathering let leaders operate objectively in the eyes of both camps before deciding anything.
Participatory Redesign — combining elements of competing options rather than picking a winner — is presented as the ultimate resolution technique.
The piece frames inflexibility, not the dispute itself, as the real threat to teams stuck on a wicked problem.
quotes: Wicked problems are complex and multi-faceted, with competing advocates that cannot escape engaging one another.

What makes a problem truly wicked isn’t just its complexity or competing choices. It is the potential for conflict and unintended relational consequences if one side were to be selected over the other.
The first step for the leader is to publicly acknowledge the complexity of the problem and how the competing sides both have a legitimate claim for selection.

Lastly and most importantly, the leader initiates Participatory Redesign. Rather than select one option over the other, they ask stakeholders and experts to explore what elements can be combined, used concurrently, or positioned for use with different audiences or times.
The only villain is the inflexibility that occurs when people are allowed to insist on their viewpoints without interruption.
